# Exercises - H Linear Time-Varying Filters

## H Linear Time-Varying Filters

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/View_Linear_Time_Varying.html

#### `ltv-basis-1` - difficulty 3; concepts: linear-time-varying, basis-expansion, filter

**Q.** The interpretation of an LTV (linear time-varying) digital filter presented here views the filter as:

- (a) A frequency-dependent gain only
- (b) An operator that replaces each input basis signal (e.g., DFT sinusoid) with an arbitrary output basis signal
- (c) A pure delay line
- (d) An allpass filter

Hint 1: LTI filters are a special case where basis signals are only scaled.

Hint 2: Matrix view: each input column is mapped to an arbitrary output column.

**Answer: (b).** Expand input in an orthogonal basis (e.g., DFT sinusoids); the LTV filter maps each basis signal independently to its own output signal. With sinusoidal basis, one can prescribe an arbitrary output waveform per input frequency.

## H Introduction

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/Introduction_I_I.html

#### `introduction-i-i-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: eigenfunctions, lti-systems, sinusoids

**Q.** Why are sinusoids called 'eigenfunctions' of linear time-invariant systems?

- (a) A stable LTI filter responds to an input sinusoid at frequency f with an output sinusoid at the same frequency f, modified only in amplitude and phase
- (b) Sinusoids pass through LTI filters completely unchanged
- (c) Sinusoids are the only signals an LTI filter can process
- (d) LTI filters convert every input into a sinusoid

Hint 1: An eigenvector is mapped to a scalar multiple of itself; here the 'scalar' is a complex gain.

Hint 2: Only the amplitude and phase can change - not the frequency.

**Answer: (a).** After start-up transients settle, a stable LTI filter emits a sinusoid at frequency f in response to an input sinusoid at frequency f: the filter can only apply a constant amplitude scaling and a constant phase offset. This is the rationale behind Fourier analysis. The sinusoid is generally changed (in amplitude and phase) - just not in frequency or shape - so option (b) is too strong.

#### `introduction-i-i-2` - difficulty 3; concepts: time-varying-filters, basis-functions, linearity

**Q.** When time-invariance is relaxed (a linear TIME-VARYING filter), how can the filter still be uniquely characterized, given that the impulse response no longer suffices?

- (a) By its basis function response - its response to each member of a basis for the signal space
- (b) By its response to a single impulse at time 0
- (c) By its dc gain alone
- (d) It cannot be characterized at all

Hint 1: Linearity survives; only superposition in time is lost.

Hint 2: Knowing the response to every basis signal determines the response to any linear combination.

**Answer: (a).** Relaxing time-invariance removes superposition in time, so one impulse response no longer determines the filter (the response depends on when the input arrives). But linearity still holds, so the filter is fully characterized by its responses to a complete set of basis functions. Moreover, since time-varying filters have no eigenfunctions, there is no fundamental reason to prefer the Fourier (sinusoidal) basis - any convenient basis for the input space may be used.

## H Derivation

Book page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/Derivation.html

#### `derivation-1` - difficulty 2; concepts: time-varying-filters, matrix-representation, causality

**Q.** In the matrix representation Y = HX of a length-3 digital filter, the general causal time-invariant filter corresponds to a matrix H with what structure?

- (a) Lower-triangular, with equal entries along each diagonal (h_0 on the main diagonal, h_1 below it, etc.)
- (b) Diagonal, with the impulse response on the diagonal
- (c) Upper-triangular, with h_0 on the main diagonal
- (d) A full matrix of independent entries h_ij

Hint 1: Causality determines which half of the matrix must be zero.

Hint 2: Time-invariance means the same impulse response is used at every time - look at the diagonals.

**Answer: (a).** Causality forces zeros above the main diagonal (the output cannot depend on future inputs), and time-invariance forces each diagonal to be constant, so H is lower-triangular with h_0 repeated on the main diagonal, h_1 on the first subdiagonal, and so on. A full matrix of independent entries (d) represents the general linear (time-varying, possibly non-causal) filter.

#### `derivation-2` - difficulty 3; concepts: time-varying-filters, dft-basis, orthogonality

**Q.** What is the key property of the 'collector matrix' C_N(k) used in decomposing a linear time-varying filter?

- (a) It annihilates all input basis components (DFT sinusoids) except the k-th
- (b) It delays the input by k samples
- (c) It inverts the DFT of the input
- (d) It scales every input component by 1/N

Hint 1: The top row of C_N(k) is a DFT basis vector; recall DFT orthogonality.

Hint 2: Applying C_N(k) to the basis signal x_j gives zero unless j = k.

**Answer: (a).** The rows of C_N(k) are built from the k-th DFT basis function, so C_N(k)x_k has every component equal to 1 while C_N(k)x_j = 0 for j ≠ k: it 'collects' only the k-th frequency component of the input and annihilates the rest. This orthogonality is what makes the decomposition G = Σ_k D(k)C_N(k) of every linear time-varying filter possible (and unique).
